Pool Pump Repair in Phoenix: What Fails and What Can Be Fixed

A pump that hums and will not start, screams on startup, drips at the seal or runs without moving water. One free call, any hour, puts you through to an independent, locally owned pool company in your part of the Valley.

Call (623) 240-0428 Rebuild or replace?
  1. Home
  2. Services
  3. Pool Pump Repair

Pool pump repair in Phoenix is usually urgent for a simple reason: when the pump stops, nothing else at the pool works. The filter stops filtering, the chlorinator stops dosing, and in summer heat the water can start to cloud within days. The good news is that a pool pump is a fairly simple machine, and many failures come down to a few replaceable parts. This page explains how the pump works, what each common symptom points to, which parts can be rebuilt, and how federal efficiency rules shape the choice when a motor needs replacing.

Phoenix Pool Cleaning Pro does not repair pumps. It is a free phone line. Call (623) 240-0428 any hour, tell the automated assistant what the pump is doing, and the call is transferred to an independent, locally owned pool company that works in your area. That company diagnoses the pump, quotes the repair and bills you directly.

How a pool pump works, part by part

Think of the pump in two halves. The motor is the electric half. The wet end, the part that touches pool water, is the plastic housing bolted to the front of it. The motor spins a shaft, and the shaft spins an impeller inside the housing. The spinning impeller throws water outward, which pulls more water in from the pool and pushes it on to the filter.

Every part on the list below can cause a different symptom, which is why a pump that "does not work" can mean five different repairs.

  • MotorThe electric drive. Older single-speed motors run at one fixed speed. Variable-speed motors have built-in electronics that let them run slower for most of the day.
  • ImpellerThe spinning vaned disc inside the housing that moves the water. Small debris, like a pebble or a seed pod, can lodge in its vanes and choke the flow.
  • DiffuserA shroud around the impeller that guides water toward the outlet.
  • Shaft sealA two-piece mechanical seal where the motor shaft passes into the wet end. It keeps water out of the motor. When it wears, water drips under the pump.
  • Strainer basketA basket in the front pot that catches leaves and debris before they reach the impeller.
  • Lid and lid O-ringThe clear or solid lid over the basket, sealed by a rubber ring. A dry, cracked or pinched O-ring lets air in, and the pump loses prime.

Pool pump symptoms and what they usually mean

Match what you hear or see to a row. The middle column is for you; the right column belongs to the technician.

Pool pump symptoms, safe homeowner checks and what a technician tests
SymptomSafe for you to checkWhat a technician looks at
Hums but will not startTurn it off so it does not overheat. Note whether it happened after a power outage.Start component on single-speed motors, seized bearings, a jammed impeller, supply voltage
Loud grinding or screechingNote when it started and whether it gets worse once the motor warms upMotor bearings, often worn after water from a leaking shaft seal reaches them
Drips or a puddle under the pumpLook where the water comes from: the lid, the fittings, or between the motor and housingShaft seal, housing O-rings, cracked fittings or a cracked housing
Runs but will not prime, or the basket fills with airWater level at the skimmer, empty baskets, the lid seated and the O-ring in placeAir leaks on the suction side, a clogged impeller, valve positions
Trips the breaker or GFCIReset once. If it trips again, leave it off.Motor windings, wiring, water in the motor, the bonding and grounding
Shuts off on hot afternoons, then restartsClear anything piled around the motor so air can reach its ventsThermal overload, a motor working too hard, poor airflow on the pad

Leave the motor, the electrical cover, the wiring and the breaker panel alone. A pump that has water in its motor or a breaker that keeps tripping is an electrical problem, and only a qualified professional should open it.

Why Phoenix pumps work so hard

Valley pools run all year, and the pump sits outside through the whole desert summer. The National Weather Service office in Phoenix recorded an average high of 110.3 degrees for July 2024, the hottest July on its record, with a peak of 117 degrees on July 8. Most equipment pads are on the sunny side of a block wall, often in a narrow side yard where hot air does not move. A motor cools itself with the air around it, so a pad stacked with leaves, boxes or a tight shade cover traps heat and makes thermal shutoffs more likely.

Debris is the other strain. Monsoon storms push dust, leaves and palm fronds into pools, and a full pump basket or a clogged impeller forces the motor to work against a blockage. Hard water adds scale inside heaters and salt cells downstream, which raises resistance in the whole system. None of this means a pump will fail on a schedule, but it explains why basket checks and clear airflow matter more here.

Rebuild the pump or replace it?

"Can a pool pump be repaired?" usually gets a yes. The question is which parts, and whether fixing them makes sense for the age of the pump.

Usually worth repairing

  • A cracked or flattened lid O-ring, or a cracked lid
  • A broken strainer basket
  • A leaking shaft seal caught before water ruins the bearings
  • A clogged or chipped impeller, or a worn diffuser
  • A failed start component on a single-speed motor
  • A worn motor on a wet end that is still in good shape

Often time to replace

  • A cracked housing or pot
  • Parts no longer made for that model
  • A burned-out motor and a worn wet end at the same time
  • A pump the wrong size for the pool and filter
  • Repeated failures from the same old unit
  • An owner who wants the energy savings of a variable-speed pump

Ask the pool company for both numbers when the choice is close: the repair now, and a replacement. Then weigh them against how long the rest of the pump is likely to last. The pool service cost guide explains what drives repair prices in the Valley. Because prices depend on the part, the motor and the company, treat any figure you read online as background and rely on the written quote.

Federal efficiency rules for pool pumps and motors

Two U.S. Department of Energy rules matter when a Phoenix pump is replaced. They apply to equipment made after the compliance dates. They do not make anyone remove a pump that still works.

U.S. Department of Energy pool pump and pool pump motor efficiency dates
DateWhat it coversWhat it means for you
July 19, 2021Dedicated-purpose pool pumps, the whole pumpNew pumps had to meet minimum efficiency levels, measured as a weighted energy factor.
September 29, 2025Pool pump motors from 1.15 to 5 total horsepowerMotors made on or after this date must have variable-speed control. This rule also reaches motors sold by themselves, the kind used when an old pump gets a new motor.
September 28, 2027Smaller motors from 0.5 to under 1.15 total horsepowerThe same variable-speed requirement for the smaller size class. In April 2026 the Department announced it would not seek penalties for these motors made before March 26, 2029, citing limited models on the market.

A variable-speed pump can run slowly for long stretches, which moves the same water with much less electricity, and speed up for vacuuming or a spa. It also needs to be set up well: the speeds and hours should suit the pool, the filter and any heater or salt cell that needs a minimum flow. Ask the technician to show you the schedule they program.

Electric bills, APS and SRP

Most Valley homes buy power from Arizona Public Service (APS) or Salt River Project (SRP), depending on the address. APS's energy-saving tips suggest running a pool pump during off-peak hours if you are on a time-of-use plan, and a variable-speed pump makes long, slow off-peak runs practical. Utility rebates come and go. SRP says its residential pool pump rebate is no longer offered, and this page did not find a current residential pool pump rebate from APS, so ask your utility before you count on one.

What a careful pool technician does on a pump call

A good pump diagnosis starts with the water side, because many "pump problems" are really suction problems. Expect the technician to check the water level and baskets, look at the lid and O-ring, watch the basket for air while the pump runs, and check the filter pressure. If the motor will not run or trips power, they test it with the right instruments instead of guessing, and check for water that has reached the motor through a failed seal. They should also look at where the pump sits: shade, airflow and clearance from walls and debris.

Good questions for the pump company

  • Is it the motor, the wet end, or something on the suction side?
  • Which parts would you replace, and can I see the old ones?
  • If you recommend a new pump, why is a repair not worth it here?
  • What speeds and hours will you set on a variable-speed pump, and why?
  • What warranty comes with the part and with your labor?
  • What is your Arizona ROC license number?

Check the license first. Arizona's Registrar of Contractors (ROC) licenses contractors, and its residential classifications include R-6, Swimming Pool Service and Repair. Routine cleaning and water care are generally not treated as contracting work, but repairs, equipment replacement and resurfacing generally call for a licensed contractor. Ask the company for its ROC license number and look it up on the ROC contractor search (opens in a new tab) before work begins. The line does not check this for you.

Common questions

Can a pool pump be repaired, or does it have to be replaced?

Many can be repaired. The lid O-ring, strainer basket, shaft seal, impeller, diffuser and housing gaskets are replaceable parts, and a worn motor can often be swapped while the wet end of the pump stays in place. Replacement makes more sense when the housing is cracked, parts are no longer available, or the motor and wet end have both failed. A pool technician who has tested the pump can tell you which case you are in.

Can pool pumps be rebuilt?

Yes, in the sense that the plumbing end of the pump can be taken apart and given new seals, gaskets and O-rings, and an impeller or diffuser can be replaced. That kind of rebuild is common when a pump leaks at the shaft seal or loses prime. Opening the motor itself, and anything to do with its wiring, is electrical work for a qualified professional, never a homeowner job.

Why does my pool pump hum but not start?

A hum with no spin usually means power is reaching the motor but it cannot turn. Common reasons are a failed start component on single-speed motors, seized bearings, or debris jamming the impeller. Turn the pump off at its switch or breaker so the motor does not overheat, and call. The motor, the shaft and the wiring are for a qualified professional to open and test.

How often should a pool pump be serviced?

The parts you can see need the most frequent attention: empty the pump basket whenever it collects debris, which can be daily after a monsoon dust storm, and check that the lid O-ring is seated and not cracked. Have a pool technician look the pump over during regular service, and sooner if it gets louder, leaks, runs hot or loses prime.

Do I have to replace my old pool pump because of the federal efficiency rules?

No. The U.S. Department of Energy standards apply to pumps and motors made after the compliance dates. They do not require anyone to remove a pump that still works. They do shape what is sold today: most pool pump motors from 1.15 to 5 total horsepower made on or after September 29, 2025 must have variable-speed control, so a replacement often ends up being a variable-speed unit.
